subject: math
title: Grade 6 Financial Literacy: Ways to Pay, Unit Price, HST and Budgets
seo_title: Grade 6 Financial Literacy Worksheets: Unit Price, 13% HST and Budgets (Free, Answer Key)
standard_text: Describe the advantages and disadvantages of various methods of payment that can be used when purchasing goods and services; determine the unit rates of goods and services, and identify which is the best value; design basic budgets
meta_desc: Free Grade 6 financial literacy math worksheets for the Ontario curriculum: cash, debit, credit and e-transfer, unit price and the best buy, adding 13% HST, cash rounding without pennies, and simple budgets for saving goals and a class trip. 100 questions with an answer key, good EQAO practice.
key_big: Compare unit prices, not totals, and add 13% HST as price × 1.13.
key_sub: The lower price per 100 g or per litre is the better buy. HST is 13¢ for every $1, rounded to the cent; only cash totals round to the nearest 5¢. A budget is balanced when money in equals money spent plus saved.
body_html:
Four ways to pay

Each way to pay has advantages and disadvantages. Choose the one that fits what you are buying.

Way to payHow it worksAdvantagesDisadvantages
CashCoins and billsYou can only spend what you have. No bank account neededCan be lost or stolen. Not for online stores. Total rounded to 5¢
Debit cardTakes money straight from your bank accountExact amount. No bill later. Works in stores and onlineNeeds a bank account. You can only spend what is in it
Credit cardBorrows money you pay back when the bill comesBuy now, pay later. Works in stores and onlineEasy to overspend. Interest is added if the bill is not paid in full on time
E-transferSends money between bank accounts by email or phone numberPay someone without meetingNeeds a bank account. A typing mistake can send money to the wrong person

Canada has no pennies. Only cash totals are rounded to the nearest 5¢ (1, 2, 6, 7 cents round down; 3, 4, 8, 9 round up). Card and e-transfer payments are exact.

Unit price: find the best buy

A bigger package usually costs more, so you cannot compare total prices. Find the unit price: the cost of the same amount, such as 100 g, 1 L or 1 item. The lower unit price is the better buy.

Adding 13% HST

In Ontario, 13% HST is added to most things you buy (some, like basic groceries, have none). 13% means 13¢ for every $1. Multiply the price by 0.13, round to the nearest cent, then add. Or multiply by 1.13 in one step.

Example

A $40.00 backpack has 13% HST added. What is the total?

HST: $40.00 × 0.13 = $5.20. Total: $40.00 + $5.20 = $45.20. One step: $40.00 × 1.13 = $45.20.

Answer: $45.20

Example

A $24.99 game has 13% HST added. How much do you pay with cash?

HST: $24.99 × 0.13 = $3.2487 → $3.25. Total: $28.24. Cash rounds to the nearest 5¢: $28.25. A card pays $28.24.

Answer: $28.25 with cash

Budgets: plan your money

A budget lists the money coming in (allowance, jobs) and the money going out (spending and saving). It is balanced when money in equals money out.

Example

You want a $90 game and save $12 a week. How many weeks will it take?

$90 ÷ $12 = 7.5. After 7 weeks you have $84, not enough. Round up.

Answer: 8 weeks

Common mistakes

MistakeWhat to do instead
Picking the package with the lower total priceCompare the price per 100 g, per litre or per item
Adding $13 (or 13¢) instead of 13%Find 13% of the price: price × 0.13
Giving only the tax as the totalAdd the HST to the price: price × 1.13
Forgetting to round a cash totalCash rounds to the nearest 5¢; cards do not
Rounding the weeks down ($90 ÷ $12 = 7.5 → 7)Round up: after 7 weeks you are still short

faq.q: What do Grade 6 students learn in financial literacy in Ontario?
faq.a: Grade 6 students compare ways to pay (cash, debit, credit and e-transfer), find unit prices to choose the best value, and design simple budgets. Money questions also use decimals and percents, such as adding 13% HST.

faq.q: How do you calculate 13% HST on a price?
faq.a: Multiply the price by 0.13 and round to the nearest cent, then add it to the price. For $40, the HST is $5.20 and the total is $45.20, the same as $40 × 1.13.

faq.q: How do you find the best buy using unit price?
faq.a: Divide each price by the amount to get the cost for the same unit, such as 100 g or 1 L. The lower unit price is the better buy, even if the package costs more in total.

faq.q: What is the difference between a debit card and a credit card?
faq.a: A debit card takes money straight from your own bank account. A credit card borrows money that you pay back later, and interest is added if the bill is not paid in full by the due date.

sets.title: Ways to pay: cash, debit, credit and e-transfer

items.q: When you pay with a debit card, where does the money come from?
c: Money borrowed from the card company
Money saved on the card itself
items.e: A debit card takes the money straight out of your own bank account when you pay. You can only spend money that is already in the account.

items.q: When you pay with a credit card, what are you doing?
c: Using money saved on the card
Taking money out of your bank account
Borrowing money to pay back later
items.e: A credit card company pays the store for you, so you are borrowing. You get a bill later and must pay it back.

items.q: Which way of paying sends money from your bank account to another person using their email address or mobile phone number?
items.e: An e-transfer moves money from one bank account to another. You send it using the other person’s email address or mobile phone number, so you do not need to meet.

items.q: Which way of paying cannot be used to buy something from an online store?
items.e: Online stores need a card or another electronic payment. You cannot hand coins and bills over the internet, so cash cannot be used.

items.q: Which way of paying is the only one where the total is rounded to the nearest 5¢?
items.e: Canada has no pennies, so only a cash total is rounded to the nearest 5¢. Debit, credit and e-transfer payments are for the exact amount.

items.q: Which way of paying can cost you interest if you do not pay the full bill by the due date?
items.e: A credit card is borrowed money. If the full bill is not paid by the due date, the card company adds interest, so the things you bought cost more.

items.q: What is one advantage of paying with cash?
c: You can only spend what you have
items.e: With cash you can see your money go down, and you cannot spend more than you have with you. Cash cannot be used online, lost cash is gone, and cash totals are rounded to 5¢.

items.q: What is one disadvantage of paying with cash?
c: It can be lost or stolen
items.e: If cash is lost or stolen, it is usually gone for good. A lost bank card can be cancelled, but coins and bills cannot.

items.q: What is one advantage of paying with a debit card?
c: You can pay the bill next month
You pay with money you already have
It never needs a bank account
items.e: Debit takes the exact amount from your bank account right away, so you pay with money you already have and do not get a bill later. You need a bank account to have a debit card.

items.q: What is one disadvantage of a debit card?
c: It cannot be used in stores
You need a bank account to use it
It only works for whole dollars
items.e: A debit card is linked to a bank account, so you need a bank account. Debit does not charge interest, because you are not borrowing.

items.q: What is one advantage of a credit card?
c: It uses only money in your account
You can buy now and pay later
You never have to pay it back
items.e: With a credit card you can buy something now and pay the bill later. If you pay the full bill by the due date, you usually pay no interest.

items.q: What is one disadvantage of a credit card?
c: It is easy to spend more than you have
items.e: Because you are borrowing, it is easy to spend more than you have. Any part of the bill not paid on time has interest added.

items.q: What is one advantage of an e-transfer?
c: You can pay without meeting in person
It gives you coins as change
It does not need a bank account
items.e: An e-transfer goes by email or phone number, so you can pay someone without meeting in person, even in another city. Both people need bank accounts.

items.q: What is one disadvantage of an e-transfer?
c: It is rounded to the nearest 5¢
A wrong email can send money astray
It can only be used in stores
items.e: If you type the wrong email address or phone number, the money can go to the wrong person, and it can be hard to get back. Always check before you send.

items.q: Amira’s grandmother in Winnipeg wants to send her $25 for her birthday. Amira lives in Halifax. Which way of paying lets her send it straight to Amira’s bank account?
items.e: An e-transfer sends money from one bank account to another using an email address or phone number. Cash would have to be mailed or handed over.

items.q: Owen buys a snack for $4.17 and pays with a debit card. How much is taken from his bank account?
items.e: Debit is charged the exact amount: $4.17. Only cash totals are rounded to 5¢.

items.q: Leah buys the same $4.17 snack and pays with cash. How much does she pay?
items.e: Cash is rounded to the nearest 5¢. $4.17 is 2¢ from $4.15 and 3¢ from $4.20, so she pays $4.15. (Totals ending in 1, 2, 6 or 7 cents round down; 3, 4, 8 or 9 round up.)

items.q: Which cash total does NOT change when it is rounded to the nearest 5¢?
Jayden’s total at the corner store is $9.48. He pays with cash. How much does he pay?
items.e: $9.48 is 2¢ from $9.50 and 3¢ from $9.45, so it rounds up to $9.50.

items.q: Hana’s total is $8.63. She pays cash with a $10 bill. How much change does she get?
items.e: Step 1, round the cash total: $8.63 is 2¢ from $8.65 and 3¢ from $8.60, so it is $8.65. Step 2, change: $10.00 − $8.65 = $1.35. ($1.37 forgets the cash rounding.)

sets.title: Unit price and the best buy

items.q: A shelf tag shows “$0.70 per 100 g”. What does this unit price tell you?
c: The cost of the whole package
The cost of 100 g of the food
items.e: A unit price is the price for one unit of the item, here 100 g. It lets you compare packages of different sizes fairly.

items.q: A 500 g bag of rice costs $3.50. What is the price per 100 g?
items.e: There are 5 groups of 100 g in 500 g, so divide: $3.50 ÷ 5 = $0.70 per 100 g. Check: $0.70 × 5 = $3.50.

items.q: A 4 L bag of milk costs $6.20. What is the price per litre?
items.e: There are 4 groups of 1 L in 4 L, so divide: $6.20 ÷ 4 = $1.55 per litre. Check: $1.55 × 4 = $6.20.

items.q: A 2 L bottle of apple juice costs $3.40. What is the price per litre?
items.e: There are 2 groups of 1 L in 2 L, so divide: $3.40 ÷ 2 = $1.70 per litre. Check: $1.70 × 2 = $3.40.

items.q: A 300 g block of cheese costs $5.40. What is the price per 100 g?
items.e: There are 3 groups of 100 g in 300 g, so divide: $5.40 ÷ 3 = $1.80 per 100 g. Check: $1.80 × 3 = $5.40.

items.q: A 1 kg bag of apples costs $4.00. What is the price per 100 g?
items.e: There are 10 groups of 100 g in 1 kg (1000 g), so divide: $4.00 ÷ 10 = $0.40 per 100 g. Check: $0.40 × 10 = $4.00. Remember 1 kg = 1000 g, not 100 g.

items.q: Two boxes of crackers are different sizes. What should you compare to find the better buy?
items.e: A bigger box usually costs more in total, so totals do not tell you which is cheaper. Compare the price for the same amount, such as per 100 g.

items.q: Which box of cereal is the better buy?
c: Both cost the same per 100 g
items.e: Compare the price per 100 g, not the total price. Box A: $6.00 ÷ 5 = $1.20 per 100 g; Box B: $8.25 ÷ 7.5 = $1.10 per 100 g. Box B has the lower price per 100 g, so it is the better buy. (Box A: lower total price, but you get less.)

items.q: Which box of crackers is the better buy?
c: Both cost the same per 100 g
items.e: Compare the price per 100 g, not the total price. Box A: $2.50 ÷ 2 = $1.25 per 100 g; Box B: $3.90 ÷ 3 = $1.30 per 100 g. Box A has the lower price per 100 g, so it is the better buy. A bigger box is not always the better buy.

items.q: Which bottle of juice is the better buy?
c: Both cost the same per litre
items.e: Compare the price per litre, not the total price. Bottle A: $2.40 ÷ 1 = $2.40 per litre; Bottle B: $4.80 ÷ 2 = $2.40 per litre. The unit prices are equal, so neither is a better buy.

items.q: Which bag of milk is the better buy?
c: Both cost the same per litre
items.e: Compare the price per litre, not the total price. Bag A: $2.60 ÷ 1 = $2.60 per litre; Bag B: $6.40 ÷ 4 = $1.60 per litre. Bag B has the lower price per litre, so it is the better buy. (Bag A: lower total price, but you get less.)

items.q: A 650 g tub of yogurt costs $3.90. A pack of 4 yogurt cups, 100 g each, costs $2.80. Which is the better buy?
c: Both cost the same per 100 g
items.e: Compare the price per 100 g, not the total price. The tub: $3.90 ÷ 6.5 = $0.60 per 100 g; The 4 cups: $2.80 ÷ 4 = $0.70 per 100 g. The tub has the lower price per 100 g, so it is the better buy. (The 4 cups: lower total price, but you get less.)

items.q: A box of 8 granola bars costs $3.20. A box of 12 granola bars costs $5.40. Which is the better buy?
c: Both cost the same per bar
items.e: Compare the price per bar, not the total price. The box of 8: $3.20 ÷ 8 = $0.40 per bar; The box of 12: $5.40 ÷ 12 = $0.45 per bar. The box of 8 has the lower price per bar, so it is the better buy.

items.q: A 500 g jar of peanut butter costs $3.50. A 1 kg jar costs $6.00. Aiden says the 500 g jar is the better buy because it costs less. Is he right?
c: No, the two jars cost the same per 100 g
Yes, smaller jars always cost less per 100 g
Yes, it costs less in total
No, the 1 kg jar costs less per 100 g
items.e: Compare unit prices, not totals. 500 g jar: $3.50 ÷ 5 = $0.70 per 100 g. 1 kg jar: $6.00 ÷ 10 = $0.60 per 100 g. The 1 kg jar costs less per 100 g, so it is the better buy (if you will use it all).

items.q: A 750 g bag of oats costs $6.00. What is the price per 100 g?
A 500 mL bottle of maple syrup costs $9.80. What is the price per litre?
items.e: 500 mL = 0.5 × 1 L, so divide: $9.80 ÷ 0.5 = $19.60 per litre. Check: $19.60 × 0.5 = $9.80. 500 mL is half a litre, so 1 L costs twice as much.

items.q: A 1.5 kg bag of carrots costs $3.45. What is the price per kilogram?
A 250 mL can of maple syrup costs $8.50. A 1 L jug costs $28.00. Which is the better buy?
c: You cannot compare mL and L
Both cost the same per litre
items.e: Compare the price per litre, not the total price. The can: $8.50 ÷ 0.25 = $34.00 per litre; The jug: $28.00 ÷ 1 = $28.00 per litre. The jug has the lower price per litre, so it is the better buy. (The can: lower total price, but you get less.)

items.q: Which jug of orange juice is the best buy?
c: They all cost the same per litre
items.e: Compare the price per litre, not the total price. Jug A: $2.80 ÷ 1 = $2.80 per litre; Jug B: $5.00 ÷ 2 = $2.50 per litre; Jug C: $10.40 ÷ 4 = $2.60 per litre. Jug B has the lowest price per litre, so it is the best buy. (Jug A: lower total price, but you get less.)

items.q: Which bag of rice is the best buy?
c: They all cost the same per 100 g
items.e: Compare the price per 100 g, not the total price. Bag A: $2.25 ÷ 5 = $0.45 per 100 g; Bag B: $4.00 ÷ 10 = $0.40 per 100 g; Bag C: $8.40 ÷ 20 = $0.42 per 100 g. Bag B has the lowest price per 100 g, so it is the best buy. (Bag A: lower total price, but you get less.)

items.q: Most things you buy in Ontario have 13% HST added. What does 13% mean?
items.e: Percent means “out of 100”. 13% = 13 out of 100, so the tax is 13¢ for every $1 of the price. On $10 the HST is $1.30.

items.q: What is 13% of $10.00?
A board game costs $20.00. How much is the 13% HST?
A pair of headphones costs $50.00. How much is the 13% HST?
A phone case costs $8.00. How much is the 13% HST?
Find 13% of $30 in your head: 10% of $30 is $3.00 and 3% of $30 is $0.90. What is 13% of $30?
Which calculation gives the total price with 13% HST in one step?
items.e: The total is 100% of the price plus 13% more = 113% = 1.13. So price × 1.13 gives the total. price × 0.13 gives only the tax.

items.q: A backpack costs $40.00. 13% HST is added. What is the total price?
A puzzle costs $25.00. 13% HST is added. What is the total price?
A skateboard costs $60.00. 13% HST is added. What is the total price?
A set of markers costs $12.40. 13% HST is added. What is the total price?
A video game costs $24.99. How much is the 13% HST, rounded to the nearest cent?
items.e: 13% = 0.13. $24.99 × 0.13 = $3.2487, which rounds to $3.25 (to the nearest cent).

items.q: A video game costs $24.99. 13% HST is added. What is the total price?
A water bottle costs $7.49. How much is the 13% HST, rounded to the nearest cent?
items.e: 13% = 0.13. $7.49 × 0.13 = $0.9737, which rounds to $0.97 (to the nearest cent).

items.q: About how much HST is added to an item that costs $79.99? Round the price first.
items.e: $79.99 is about $80. 10% of $80 is $8 and 3% is $2.40, so 13% is about $8 + $2.40 = $10.40. ($8 is only 10%; $13 adds $13 instead of 13%.)

items.q: A $7.00 key chain has 13% HST added. Noah pays with cash. How much does he pay?
items.e: HST: $7.00 × 0.13 = $0.91. Total: $7.91. Cash is rounded to the nearest 5¢: $7.91 → $7.90. ($7.91 is what a card pays.)

items.q: A $3.60 pack of trading cards has 13% HST added. Ethan pays with cash. How much does he pay?
A soccer ball costs $14.99 and a pump costs $5.00. 13% HST is added to the total. What is the total price?
A pack of art paper costs $15.75. How much is the 13% HST, rounded to the nearest cent?
items.e: 13% = 0.13. $15.75 × 0.13 = $2.0475, which rounds to $2.05 (to the nearest cent). Do not just cut off the extra digits ($2.04): 0.75¢ rounds up.

items.q: A total of $11.30 includes 13% HST. What was the price before HST?
items.e: The total is 113% of the price, so price × 1.13 = $11.30. Price = $11.30 ÷ 1.13 = $10.00. Check: $10.00 + $1.30 = $11.30. ($9.83 takes 13% of the total, but the tax was 13% of the price. $12.77 adds the tax a second time.)

items.q: What is a budget?
c: A list of things you want to buy
The money in your bank account
A plan for earning, spending and saving
items.e: A budget is a plan for your money: the money coming in (earning) and how it will be spent and saved.

items.q: When is a budget balanced?
c: Money in = money spent + money saved
Money spent is more than money in
items.e: A budget is balanced when every dollar coming in is planned for: spending plus saving equals money in.

items.q: Emma gets a $15 allowance each week and saves $5 of it. How much has she saved after 6 weeks?
items.e: She saves $5 each week. 6 × $5 = $30. ($90 is all of the allowance, and $60 is the part spent.)

items.q: Arjun earns $12 an hour babysitting. On Saturday he babysits for 3.5 hours. How much does he earn?
items.e: Earnings = rate × hours = $12 × 3.5. $12 × 3 = $36 and $12 × 0.5 = $6. $36 + $6 = $42. ($36 leaves out the half hour.)

items.q: Nathan wants headphones that cost $84. He saves $12 each week. How many weeks will it take?
items.e: Divide the goal by the savings each week: $84 ÷ $12 = 7 weeks. Check: 7 × $12 = $84. (72 comes from subtracting $84 − $12.)

items.q: Mateo wants a video game that costs $90. He saves $12 each week. How many weeks until he has enough?
items.e: $90 ÷ $12 = 7.5. After 7 weeks he has only 7 × $12 = $84, which is not enough. After 8 weeks he has $96. So it takes 8 weeks: round up.

items.q: Kai plans to save 25% of a $20 allowance. How much does he save?
items.e: 25% is one quarter. $20 ÷ 4 = $5. ($15 is the 75% he keeps to spend.)

items.q: Sofia earns $40. She plans to save 50%, spend 30% and give 20% to charity. How much will she spend?
items.e: Spend 30% of $40: 10% is $4, so 30% is 3 × $4 = $12. Check: save $20 + spend $12 + give $8 = $40.

items.q: Look at Olivia’s budget. How much money is not planned for yet?
items.e: Money in: $20 + $15 = $35. Money out: $12 + $6 + $10 = $28 (savings is planned money too). $35 − $28 = $7. ($17 forgets to count the savings.)

items.q: Is Lucas’s budget balanced?
c: No, he plans $55 more than he has
No, he plans $5 more than he has
items.e: Money out: $18 + $15 + $22 = $55. Money in: $50. $55 − $50 = $5, so he plans to spend and save $5 more than he has. He could save $17 instead of $22.

items.q: A Grade 6 class of 28 students is going on a field trip. The bus costs $420. How much is the bus for each student?
items.e: Share the cost equally: $420 ÷ 28 = $15. Check: 28 × $15 = $420.

items.q: Admission to the science centre is $12.50 per student. How much is admission for all 28 students?
For the field trip, each student pays $15 for the bus and $12.50 for admission. What is the total for each student?
The class raises $252 at a bake sale to help pay for the $27.50-per-student trip. The money is shared equally by the 28 students. How much does each student pay now?
Maya can earn $3 for each day of chores (6 days a week), or get $20 each week. Which choice gives more money in a week?
items.e: $3 × 6 days = $18 a week. $20 > $18, so $20 each week gives $2 more.

items.q: Mei has $35 saved. She wants a bike helmet that costs $110 and saves $15 each week. How many more weeks until she can buy it?
items.e: She still needs $110 − $35 = $75. $75 ÷ $15 = 5 weeks. (8 weeks forgets the $35 already saved.)

items.q: After a big snowfall, Priya shovels 7 driveways at $20 each. She spends $45 on new winter mitts and a hat. How much does she have left to save?
A budget lists needs and wants. In a Canadian winter, which is a need for a student?
items.e: A need is something you must have to be safe and healthy. Winter boots that fit keep your feet warm and dry. The others are wants: nice to have, but not needed.

items.q: Chloe’s budget is $48 for the month. She plans to spend $12 on snacks. What percent of the budget is that?
items.e: $12 out of $48 = 12/48 = 1/4 = 25%. (12% uses the dollars as the percent; 4% comes from 48 ÷ 12.)

items.q: Benjamin wants to save $150 for summer camp by Canada Day, which is 10 weeks away. How much must he save each week?
items.e: Share the goal over the weeks: $150 ÷ 10 = $15 a week. Check: 10 × $15 = $150.

items.q: Ava buys a hockey stick for $59.99. 13% HST is added, and she pays with a debit card. How much is she charged?
items.e: HST: $59.99 × 0.13 = $7.7987 → $7.80. Total: $59.99 + $7.80 = $67.79. Debit is charged the exact amount, so it is not rounded to 5¢.

items.q: Zoe buys a $21.00 board game. 13% HST is added, and she pays with cash. How much does she pay?
items.e: HST: $21.00 × 0.13 = $2.73. Total: $23.73. Cash: $23.73 is 2¢ from $23.75, so she pays $23.75. ($23.73 forgets the cash rounding.)

items.q: Liam buys a $16.00 art kit. 13% HST is added. He pays cash with a $20 bill. How much change does he get?
items.e: HST: $16.00 × 0.13 = $2.08, so the total is $18.08. Cash rounds $18.08 up to $18.10. Change: $20.00 − $18.10 = $1.90. ($1.92 forgets the cash rounding; $4.00 forgets the HST.)

items.q: Amira wants a skateboard that costs $80 plus 13% HST. She has $15 saved and saves $10 each week. How many more weeks until she can buy it?
items.e: Total with HST: $80 × 1.13 = $90.40. Still needed: $90.40 − $15 = $75.40. $75.40 ÷ $10 = 7.54, so round up to 8 weeks. (7 weeks forgets the HST; 10 weeks forgets the $15 saved.)

items.q: Owen needs 15 notebooks for school. Store A sells 3 notebooks for $4.50. Store B sells 5 notebooks for $7.00. How much does he save by buying them all at the store with the lower unit price?
items.e: Unit prices: Store A $4.50 ÷ 3 = $1.50 each; Store B $7.00 ÷ 5 = $1.40 each. 15 notebooks: Store A 15 × $1.50 = $22.50; Store B 15 × $1.40 = $21.00. Savings: $22.50 − $21.00 = $1.50.

items.q: A $48 hoodie is on sale for 25% off. What is the sale price before tax?
items.e: 25% of $48 = $48 ÷ 4 = $12 off. Sale price: $48 − $12 = $36. ($12 is the discount, not the price.)

items.q: Leah buys the hoodie at the sale price of $36. 13% HST is added. What is the total?
For the Terry Fox Run, 4 neighbours each pledge $2.50 for every kilometre Jayden runs. He runs 5 km. How much does he raise?
items.e: One neighbour gives 5 × $2.50 = $12.50. Four neighbours give 4 × $12.50 = $50.

items.q: Hana and 3 friends order pizza for $54.24, tax included. Hana pays, and her friends send their shares by e-transfer. What is each person’s equal share?
items.e: Hana and 3 friends make 4 people. $54.24 ÷ 4 = $13.56. (Dividing by 3 forgets to count Hana.) Check: 4 × $13.56 = $54.24.

items.q: Aiden has $50 in his bank account. He buys $32.00 earbuds with a debit card, and 13% HST is added. How much is left in the account?
items.e: HST: $32 × 0.13 = $4.16. Total: $36.16. Left: $50.00 − $36.16 = $13.84. Debit is exact, so there is no rounding. ($18 forgets the HST.)

items.q: Each Saturday Noah babysits for 4 hours at $13 an hour. He wants to earn $156 for a new bike. How many Saturdays will it take?
items.e: Each Saturday: 4 × $13 = $52. $156 ÷ $52 = 3 Saturdays. (12 divides by $13, the pay for only one hour.)

items.q: Apples are sold in three bags. Which bag is the best buy?
c: They all cost the same per kilogram
items.e: Compare the price per kilogram, not the total price. Bag A: $5.20 ÷ 2 = $2.60 per kilogram; Bag B: $7.50 ÷ 3 = $2.50 per kilogram; Bag C: $13.00 ÷ 5 = $2.60 per kilogram. Bag B has the lowest price per kilogram, so it is the best buy. (Bag A: lower total price, but you get less.)

items.q: A class orders 6 pizzas at $15 each for a pizza lunch. 13% HST is added. What is the total cost?
Ethan buys a basketball for $27.99. 13% HST is added. He pays cash with a $50 bill. How much change does he get?
items.e: HST: $27.99 × 0.13 = $3.6387 → $3.64. Total: $31.63. Cash rounds $31.63 up to $31.65. Change: $50.00 − $31.65 = $18.35. ($22.01 forgets the HST; $18.37 forgets the cash rounding.)

items.q: A family pays $62.00 for 40 L of gas on the drive to the cottage. At the same price per litre, how much would 50 L cost?
items.e: Unit price: $62.00 ÷ 40 = $1.55 per litre. 50 L: 50 × $1.55 = $77.50. ($72 adds $10 for 10 more litres instead of 10 × $1.55.)

items.q: Emma earns $15 a week and saves 40% of it. How many weeks will it take her to save $54?
items.e: 40% of $15: 10% is $1.50, so 40% is 4 × $1.50 = $6 a week. $54 ÷ $6 = 9 weeks. (4 weeks uses all $15; 6 is the dollars saved each week, not the weeks.)

items.q: Arjun buys a $2.98 granola bar with cash. Nathan buys the same bar with a debit card. Who pays more, and by how much?
items.e: Cash: $2.98 rounds up to $3.00. Debit: exactly $2.98. Arjun pays 2¢ more. On another day a cash total might round down instead, so cash can also cost a little less.

items.q: A class of 26 students goes on a field trip. The bus costs $650 and admission is $14 per student. The school council gives $260. The rest is shared equally. How much does each student pay?
items.e: Bus per student: $650 ÷ 26 = $25. Cost per student: $25 + $14 = $39. Council money per student: $260 ÷ 26 = $10. Each pays $39 − $10 = $29.

items.q: Public skating costs $6 a visit, or $75 for a winter pass. Mateo plans to skate 15 times this winter. Which is cheaper, and by how much?
items.e: Paying each visit: 15 × $6 = $90. The pass: $75. $90 − $75 = $15, so the pass is cheaper by $15. ($69 is $75 − $6.)
